title: What is a Source Connector vs a Sink Connector — Source reads from an external system (database, file, API) and writes to Kafka; Sink reads from Kafka and writes to an external system (S3, database, Elasticsearch)?
shortTitle: What is a Source Connector vs a Sink Connector?

s1_definition.profdef: In Kafka Connect, a Source Connector and a Sink Connector are the two directions of data movement. A Source Connector reads from an external system such as a database, a file, or an API, and writes the data into Kafka topics, so Kafka is the destination. A Sink Connector reads from Kafka topics and writes the data out to an external system such as object storage, a database, or a search index, so Kafka is the origin. The simplest way to remember it is that source produces into Kafka and sink consumes from Kafka.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Kafka as the central sorting office at National Bank of India. A source connector is the intake clerk who walks out to the account database, collects new records, and brings them into the sorting office. A sink connector is the dispatch clerk who takes sorted records out of the office and files them into cloud storage or a search index. The intake clerk fills the office; the dispatch clerk empties it to somewhere useful. Data always flows through the sorting office in between.
s1_definition.oneliner: A source connector writes external data into Kafka; a sink connector writes Kafka data out to an external system.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Kafka Connect, a Source Connector and a Sink Connector are the two directions of data movement. A Source Connector reads from an external system such as a database, a file, or an API, and writes the data into Kafka topics, so Kafka is the destination. A Sink Connector reads from Kafka topics and writes the data out to an external system such as object storage, a database, or a search index, so Kafka is the origin. The simplest way to remember it is that source produces into Kafka and sink consumes from Kafka.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Kafka as the central sorting office at National Bank of India. A source connector is the intake clerk who walks out to the account database, collects new records, and brings them into the sorting office. A sink connector is the dispatch clerk who takes sorted records out of the office and files them into cloud storage or a search index. The intake clerk fills the office; the dispatch clerk empties it to somewhere useful. Data always flows through the sorting office in between.

**One line to remember:** A source connector writes external data into Kafka; a sink connector writes Kafka data out to an external system.

sections.s2_technical:
A Source Connector is on the import side. It talks to an external system and turns its data into Kafka records. Internally it implements a poll method that returns a batch of source records, and the Connect runtime produces those into topics. A JDBC source polls tables by an incrementing id or a timestamp; a file source tails files; an API source calls an endpoint on a schedule; and a change-data-capture source reads the database transaction log. The key behaviour is that the connector tracks a source offset, which is its own notion of position in the external system, such as the last row id read, stored by Connect in an internal topic, so after a restart it resumes from exactly where it stopped rather than re-importing everything.

A Sink Connector is on the export side. It is effectively a managed Kafka consumer that reads records from one or more topics and writes them to an external system. Internally it implements a put method that receives a batch of records to write, and a flush that commits progress. An S3 sink buffers records and writes files; a JDBC sink upserts rows into a database; an Elasticsearch sink indexes documents. The crucial behaviour is ordering of operations: it writes to the external system first and commits the Kafka consumer offsets only after the write succeeds, so a crash cannot lose records, giving at-least-once delivery to the target.

The symmetry is the easiest mental model. Source: external system to Kafka, Kafka is the destination, the connector is like a producer. Sink: Kafka to external system, Kafka is the origin, the connector is like a consumer. Both are pure configuration for standard systems, and both benefit from the runtime's scaling into tasks, fault tolerance, and automatic offset handling, but they track different kinds of offset: a source tracks its position in the external system, while a sink tracks its position in Kafka.

In a real pipeline you often chain a source and a sink to bridge two systems through Kafka. For example a JDBC source brings account changes into a topic, and an S3 sink archives that same topic to object storage, so the database is mirrored to a data lake with no custom code. The senior nuances are that converters apply symmetrically, with a source serializing into the wire format and a sink deserializing from it, so both ends must agree on JSON, Avro, or Protobuf; that a sink is at-least-once by default, so the target should be idempotent, for example a JDBC sink using upsert semantics keyed by a primary key so a replay does not duplicate; that single-message transforms can reshape records in either direction; and that choosing the right source mode, such as timestamp-plus-incrementing for databases, matters to avoid missing or duplicating rows.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that account changes in the operational database must become searchable in near real time and also mirrored into another database for reporting, all through Kafka.

Problem 1 — the operations team needs every change to the accounts table to enter Kafka automatically. This is exactly what a Source Connector does: it reads new rows and writes them into a Kafka topic, tracking the last id so it never re-imports old rows.

Problem 2 — the search team needs those same records indexed in a search engine so staff can look up accounts instantly. This is exactly what a Sink Connector does: it reads the topic and writes each record into the search index, committing Kafka offsets only after indexing succeeds.

Problem 3 — the reporting team needs the same records upserted into a separate reporting database, and a replay must not create duplicates. This is exactly what a Sink Connector with upsert semantics keyed by account id provides.

The code will model a `SourceConnector` that reads an accounts table and produces to a topic while tracking a source offset, and two `SinkConnector` variants, one that indexes into a search store and one that upserts into a reporting store keyed by account id, each tracking its Kafka offset and writing before committing. The demo step is: import two accounts via the source, index and upsert them via the sinks, then import a new account and replay one record to show the upsert deduplicates.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,         -- source incrementing column
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Reporting DB target for the JDBC sink (upsert keyed by account_id).
CREATE TABLE report_accounts (
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,     -- upsert key → replay-safe
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, account_id, holder_name, balance) VALUES
    (1, 'SAV2001', 'Rajesh Kumar', 1000000.00),
    (2, 'CUR3001', 'Priya Sharma', 250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# connectors/accounts-source.json
# { "name":"accounts-source","config":{
#     "connector.class":"io.confluent.connect.jdbc.JdbcSourceConnector",
#     "table.whitelist":"accounts","mode":"incrementing",
#     "incrementing.column.name":"id","topic.prefix":"bank." } }

# connectors/accounts-report-sink.json  (upsert → replay-safe)
# { "name":"accounts-report-sink","config":{
#     "connector.class":"io.confluent.connect.jdbc.JdbcSinkConnector",
#     "topics":"bank.accounts","insert.mode":"upsert",
#     "pk.mode":"record_key","pk.fields":"account_id" } }
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is an accounts table with Rajesh and Priya, which must be mirrored into a search index and a reporting database through Kafka.

Step 1: The source connector polls the table from a source offset of zero and reads both rows. It produces them into the Kafka topic and advances its source offset to two, which is its position in the external database.

Step 2: The search sink consumes the topic from its Kafka offset of zero, indexes both records into the search store, and commits its Kafka offset to two only after indexing succeeds.

Step 3: The report sink independently consumes the topic from its own Kafka offset of zero, upserts both records into the reporting database keyed by account id, and commits its offset to two.

Step 4: A new account for Amit is inserted at id three. The source connector polls again, reads only rows newer than its saved source offset of two, and produces just Amit into the topic.

Step 5: The report sink consumes the new record and upserts Amit, then a redelivery of the last record is simulated. Because the sink upserts by account id, the replay updates the existing Amit row rather than inserting a duplicate, demonstrating replay-safe at-least-once.

Step 6: The final state shows three records in the topic, matching documents in search, and three rows in the reporting database with no duplicate despite the replay.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Source vs Sink Connector Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Adapter: Source adapts DB→records; Sink adapts records→target     │
  │ Checkpoint: source offset (external position) vs sink offset (Kafka)│
  │ Idempotent Receiver: report sink upserts by account_id            │
  │   WHY: at-least-once replay must not duplicate                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: source imports; each sink exports to one target                │
  │ O: new target = new sink config, pipeline unchanged               │
  │ D: sink depends on a write function, not a concrete target SDK     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ SourceConnector          │───────▶│ Topic                     │
  │ - sourceOffsetLastId     │ append │ + append/from/last/size   │
  │ + poll()                 │        └───────────┬──────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────┘          consumed │
  ┌──────────────────────────┐                   ▼
  │ SinkConnector            │        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ - kafkaOffset            │───────▶│ SearchStore / ReportStore │
  │ + consume() / replayLast │ write  │ + index / upsert          │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: offsets ─────────────────────────────────────────

  SOURCE: [extPos=0] ──poll──→ [extPos=2] ──new──→ [extPos=3]
  SINK:   [kOff=0] ──write+commit──→ [kOff=2] ──write+commit──→ [kOff=3]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. source.poll() → produce id 1,2 → topic size 2
  2. searchSink.consume() → index 2 → kOff 2
  3. reportSink.consume() → upsert 2 → kOff 2
  4. db.insert(id 3); source.poll() → produce id 3
  5. reportSink.consume() → upsert Amit; replayLast() → upsert again → still 1 row
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A source connector and a sink connector are the two directions of Kafka Connect, and the cleanest way to hold it in your head is that source produces into Kafka while sink consumes from Kafka. A source connector reads from an external system, a database, a file, or an API, and writes that data into Kafka topics, so Kafka is the destination and the connector behaves like a managed producer. A sink connector reads from Kafka topics and writes the data out to an external system such as object storage, a database, or a search index, so Kafka is the origin and the connector behaves like a managed consumer.

A detail interviewers like is that the two track different kinds of offset. A source tracks its position in the external system, for example the last row id it read, which Connect stores so it resumes from exactly there after a restart and never re-imports old rows. A sink tracks its position in Kafka, the consumer offset, and crucially it writes to the external target first and commits that Kafka offset only after the write succeeds, which gives at-least-once delivery so a crash never loses records.

In the account-mirroring pipeline at National Bank of India I chained both. A JDBC source brought every change to the accounts table into a topic, tracking the last id so restarts were clean, and then two sinks fed off that one topic independently, each with its own Kafka offset: an Elasticsearch sink made accounts instantly searchable, and a JDBC sink mirrored them into a reporting database. Because the reporting sink upserted keyed by account id, a redelivery of Amit's record under at-least-once simply updated the existing row instead of creating a duplicate.

The senior nuances I add are that converters apply symmetrically, so the source serializes into JSON, Avro, or Protobuf and the sink deserializes from the same format, which means both ends must agree, often with a schema registry for Avro; that a sink is at-least-once by default so the target should be idempotent, typically through upsert semantics keyed by a primary key; that single-message transforms can reshape records in either direction; and that choosing the right source polling mode, such as timestamp-plus-incrementing for a database, is what prevents missed or duplicated rows on the import side.

---

keyPoints: Kafka Connect: move data between Kafka and external systems
Source connector: DB/file -> Kafka. Sink connector: Kafka -> DB/file
Debezium: CDC (Change Data Capture) source connector
Distributed mode: scalable, fault-tolerant connector deployment
